caption: Figure 17.0.1: Human preferences steer model behavior: judges score outputs, and the model gradually learns to be helpful, harmless, and honest.
Figure 17.1.1: RLHF is basically a talent show for language models. Humans judge the performances, and the model learns to play to the crowd.

Figure 17.1.2a: The RL fine-tuning step of RLHF. The language model generates responses scored by a reward model, and PPO optimizes the policy to maximize reward while staying close to the original distribution via a KL penalty. (Source: Lambert et al., "Illustrating RLHF", Hugging Face Blog, 2023.)

Figure 17.1.2b: The complete three-stage RLHF pipeline. Stage 1 produces an SFT model from instruction data. Stage 2 trains a reward model on human preference comparisons. Stage 3 uses PPO to optimize the policy against the reward model while staying close to the SFT distribution. (Source: Chip Huyen, "RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback", 2023.)
Figure 17.2.1: DPO looks at Section 17.1's elaborate setup and says: why hire a separate critic when the model can learn directly from preferences? Fewer moving parts, similar results.
Figure 17.3.1: Constitutional AI gives the model its own moral compass. Instead of relying solely on human feedback, the model critiques itself against a set of principles.
Figure 19.0.1: Words that mean similar things cluster together in embedding space, like guests at a party who naturally find their conversational soulmates.
Figure 19.1.1: Welcome to the embedding space party, where similar concepts hang out together and unrelated ones awkwardly avoid each other across the room.
Figure 19.1.2: Contrastive learning works like magnets: similar pairs get pulled together while dissimilar ones get pushed apart. Simple physics, powerful embeddings.
Figure 19.1.3: Matryoshka embeddings are like Russian nesting dolls: peel off outer dimensions and you still get a useful (if smaller) representation inside.
Figure 19.2.1: HNSW navigates vector space like a city driver: start on the highway for big jumps, then switch to local streets to find the exact address.
Figure 19.2.2: Product quantization is like painting with a limited palette. You cannot represent every exact shade, but a clever mix of base colors gets surprisingly close.
Figure 19.2.3: The upper layers of HNSW are express lanes that skip most stops. The lower layers handle the last-mile navigation to your nearest neighbors.
Figure 19.3.1: A vector database librarian does not care about alphabetical order. They shelve books by vibes, so everything about cooking ends up near everything about food.
Figure 19.3.2: Metadata filtering is the bouncer of vector search. Before any similarity matching happens, it checks the tags and kicks out vectors that do not belong.
Figure 19.4.1: Chunking a document is like slicing a baguette. Too thin and you lose context; too thick and it will not fit in the model's mouth.
Figure 19.4.2: Semantic chunking is sushi-grade precision. Cut at the natural boundaries, not at arbitrary character counts, and every piece is a complete thought.
Figure 19.4.3: Parent-child retrieval: search finds the specific detail (child chunk), then hands back the full context (parent chunk). Zoom in to find it, zoom out to understand it.
Figure 19.5.1: ColPali gives retrieval systems X-ray vision for documents. Instead of just reading the text, it sees the whole page layout, tables, figures, and all.
Figure 19.5.2: Late interaction models let each query token independently interrogate every document token. It is like having a panel of specialist judges instead of one generalist.
Figure 20.0.1: RAG is the open-book exam of AI: instead of memorizing everything, the model looks up what it needs and weaves the answer on the fly.
Figure 20.2.1: Advanced RAG is a treasure hunt where each retrieval step gets you closer to the answer. Query rewriting, re-ranking, and iterative refinement are your map and compass.
Figure 20.2.2: Reranking is the callback round: initial retrieval gives you candidates, then a cross-encoder judge takes a closer look at each one to pick the real winners.

Figure 20.2.3: HyDE peers into a crystal ball to generate a hypothetical answer first, then uses that answer to find real documents. Sometimes the best search query is a rough draft of the answer itself.
Figure 20.2.4: The lost-in-the-middle problem: LLMs pay attention to the first and last documents but forget what is sandwiched in between. Position matters more than it should.
Figure 20.3.1: Knowledge graphs turn your documents into connected islands of facts. Each bridge is a relationship, and RAG can traverse them to find answers that span multiple hops.
Figure 20.3.2: Navigating a knowledge graph is like riding the subway: hop between entity stations along relationship lines to reach your destination answer.
Figure 20.3.3: GraphRAG turns your retrieval system into a detective. Pin the entities to the board, connect them with strings, and follow the relationships to crack the case.
Figure 20.4.1: Agentic RAG iterates through search, evaluation, and refinement cycles until the full picture emerges.
Figure 21.0.1: Great conversational AI never forgets your preferences, juggles multiple topics at once, and always knows when to hand you off to a specialist.
Figure 21.1.1: The best dialogue systems juggle multiple conversations, remember preferences, and route requests without dropping a single thread.
Figure 21.3.1: Memory management in conversational AI: short-term memory holds the current chat, long-term memory stores user preferences, and working memory juggles it all without spilling.
Figure 22.1.1: The agent control room: observe the environment, plan the next move, execute an action, and repeat. It is an endless loop of perceive, think, act.
Figure 22.1.2: The agent loop as detective work: perceive clues, reason about suspects, act on leads, then observe the results and start again.
Figure 22.1.3: Four agentic design patterns define the modern agent landscape: reflection, tool use, planning, and multi-agent coordination. Most real systems combine several.
Figure 23.1.1: An AI agent selects from a structured toolkit rather than improvising. Each tool comes with a schema that defines its interface, enabling reliable function calling.

Figure 23.1.2: The function calling loop in action. The model sends a structured request, the application executes the tool, and the result feeds back into the next model turn. The cycle repeats until the model has enough information to respond.

Figure 23.2.1: MCP as a universal connector for AI agents. Just as USB standardized peripheral connections, MCP provides a single protocol through which agents access databases, browsers, calendars, and code editors.
Figure 23.3.1: The A2A protocol enables independent agents to discover each other, advertise their capabilities, and coordinate on shared tasks through structured message exchange.
Figure 23.4.1: Good tool design versus bad. A monolithic multi-purpose tool confuses the agent, while atomic, well-labeled tools with clear boundaries make selection straightforward.

Figure 23.5.1: Agentic RAG plans, evaluates, and iterates on its retrieval strategy, unlike static RAG which executes a single fixed query. The agentic librarian consults a map, marks relevant shelves, and rejects poor sources.
Figure 24.1.1: Multi-agent orchestration resembles a robot orchestra: specialized agents each play their part, while a conductor coordinates the ensemble into a coherent performance.

Figure 24.2.1: Three foundational multi-agent topologies. Hub and spoke (supervisor), pipeline (sequential handoff), and fully connected mesh each offer different trade-offs between control, simplicity, and flexibility.

Figure 24.3.1: Human-in-the-loop oversight with graduated autonomy. Low-risk decisions (gold star) pass through automatically, while high-consequence actions require explicit human approval at the control panel.
